subChunks.title: Special & General Relativity
subChunks.hookHtml:
Theodora spread a sheet of paper across the table and drew a single straight line. “Before Einstein,” she said, “everyone agreed on what this line means: time, flowing at the same rate for every observer in the universe. Newton built his entire mechanics on it. It felt like bedrock.” She crumpled the paper into a ball. “Einstein noticed the bedrock was floating.”

The two theories of relativity — special (1905) and general (1915) — are among the most conceptually radical achievements in the history of science. They do not merely refine Newtonian mechanics; they replace its foundations. Time is not universal. Space is not a fixed stage. Gravity is not a force. And yet relativity's predictions agree with experiment to extraordinary precision: GPS satellites require relativistic corrections to remain accurate, gravitational waves were detected exactly as Einstein's equations predicted, and the image of a black hole shadow matches general relativistic simulations to within measurement uncertainty.

At SENIOR level, your task is not simply to know what relativity predicts but to understand why the postulates lead to those predictions, to work with the key equations quantitatively, and to evaluate relativity's conceptual implications critically. Einstein overturned two centuries of certainty. He did it by noticing an inconsistency nobody else took seriously — and following the mathematics wherever it led.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Special Relativity — The Two Postulates

Special relativity rests on two postulates Einstein stated in 1905:

  1. Principle of relativity: The laws of physics are the same in all inertial (non-accelerating) reference frames.
  2. Constancy of the speed of light: The speed of light in a vacuum, c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, is the same for all inertial observers regardless of the motion of the source or observer.

The second postulate directly contradicts Galilean velocity addition. If a train moving at 0.9c fires a laser forward, Newtonian mechanics would say the light travels at 1.9c relative to a platform observer. But it does not: both the train passenger and the platform observer measure the same speed c. This seems paradoxical until you accept that space and time are not independently fixed — they adjust to preserve the speed of light.

Time Dilation

Consider a “light clock” aboard a moving spaceship: a photon bouncing vertically between two mirrors separated by distance d. For a passenger, the photon travels distance 2d per tick. For a ground observer watching the ship pass horizontally, the photon traces a longer diagonal path. Since the speed of light is constant, each tick must take longer as measured from the ground. The result is:

Δt = γΔt₀

where Δt₀ is the proper time (measured in the frame where the clock is at rest), Δt is the dilated time measured by a moving observer, and γ (the Lorentz factor) is:

γ = 1 / √(1 − v²/c²)

At v = 0.6c, γ = 1.25: a clock on the spaceship runs 25% slower as measured from Earth. At v = 0.99c, γ ≈ 7.09. The effect is negligible at everyday speeds but measurable with atomic clocks aboard aircraft (Hafele-Keating experiment, 1971) and is built into GPS clock corrections.

Length Contraction

Moving objects are measured as shorter in the direction of motion:

L = L₀ / γ

where L₀ is the proper length (rest length). A spaceship of rest length 100 m travelling at 0.6c appears to a ground observer as 80 m long. Note that this is a real measurement difference, not an illusion — but the crew experiences their ship as its full 100 m. There is no contradiction because simultaneity is also relative.

Relativity of Simultaneity

Events that are simultaneous in one frame are not simultaneous in another. If two lightning bolts strike the front and back of a moving train simultaneously as measured by a platform observer, the passenger (moving toward the front strike) measures the front bolt hitting first. This is not about light travel time delays — it is a fundamental feature of spacetime. It makes the universe's past, present, and future frame-dependent.

Lorentz Transformations

The full mathematical framework relates coordinates between frames. For a frame S′ moving at velocity v along the x-axis relative to frame S:

  • x′ = γ(x − vt)
  • t′ = γ(t − vx/c²)

These replace the Galilean transformations (x′ = x − vt, t′ = t). At v ≪ c, γ → 1 and we recover classical mechanics.

Mass–Energy Equivalence

From special relativity emerges the most famous equation in physics:

E = mc²

More completely, the total energy of a moving object is E = γmc². The rest energy E₀ = mc² is energy contained purely in mass. A kilogram of matter contains ~9 × 10¹⁶ J — equivalent to ~21 megatons of TNT. Kinetic energy is K = (γ − 1)mc². Importantly, no massive particle can reach c: as v → c, γ → ∞, requiring infinite energy. Massless particles (photons) travel at exactly c.

General Relativity — Gravity as Geometry

Special relativity applies only to inertial frames. General relativity (GR), published in 1915, extends the framework to accelerating frames and provides a new theory of gravity. Its central insight is Einstein's equivalence principle: a gravitational field is locally indistinguishable from an accelerating reference frame. There is no experiment you can perform in a sealed box that distinguishes between resting on Earth's surface and accelerating upward at 9.81 m s⁻² in space.

From this insight, Einstein deduced that gravity is not a force acting between masses through space — it is the curvature of spacetime caused by mass and energy. Objects in free fall follow the straightest possible paths (geodesics) through curved spacetime, which we observe as the parabolic trajectories of projectiles or the elliptical orbits of planets.

Predictions and Confirmations of GR

Mercury's precessing perihelion: Newton's gravity predicted Mercury's orbit should trace a closed ellipse. In reality its ellipse slowly rotates (precesses) by 43 arcseconds per century — unexplained until GR, which predicts exactly this value from the curvature of spacetime near the Sun.

Gravitational lensing: Light follows geodesics in curved spacetime; near massive objects it bends. Eddington's 1919 solar eclipse expedition measured the deflection of starlight by the Sun (1.75 arcseconds), matching GR's prediction and twice Newton's value. The Hubble Space Telescope has since photographed Einstein rings — perfect circles formed when a galaxy exactly aligns a background source with Earth.

Gravitational time dilation: Clocks at lower gravitational potential run slower than clocks at higher potential. This is distinct from (and additive with) the velocity-based dilation of SR. GPS satellites experience both effects: SR slows their clocks by ~7 μs/day; GR speeds them up by ~45 μs/day (they are higher, thus in weaker gravity). The net +38 μs/day correction is applied continuously. Without it, GPS positions would drift ~10 km/day.

Gravitational redshift: Photons escaping a gravitational well lose energy, shifting to longer wavelengths. Measured directly in the Pound-Rebka experiment (1959) using gamma rays over a 22.5 m height difference.

Gravitational waves: Accelerating masses create ripples in spacetime, propagating at c. LIGO detected the first gravitational wave event (GW150914) in September 2015 — two black holes of ~29 and ~36 solar masses merging 1.3 billion light years away. The signal matched GR predictions precisely.

Black holes: When a sufficiently massive star collapses, spacetime curvature becomes extreme. Beyond the event horizon — the Schwarzschild radius r_s = 2GM/c² — no light or matter can escape. The Event Horizon Telescope imaged the shadow of M87's supermassive black hole (2019) and Sagittarius A* (2022), both consistent with GR.

Conceptual Implications and Limits

Relativity challenges our intuitions built from everyday experience at low velocities and weak gravity. Time travel to the future is not science fiction — it happens whenever you move fast relative to another observer. The twin paradox (one twin travels at relativistic speed, returns younger) is fully consistent with SR once acceleration is properly handled.

GR predicts its own limits: at the singularity inside a black hole, spacetime curvature diverges and the theory breaks down. A complete theory of quantum gravity — reconciling GR with quantum mechanics — remains one of the deepest unsolved problems in physics. String theory and loop quantum gravity are candidate frameworks, but neither has yet produced testable predictions that distinguish it from alternatives.

storyBeats.text: Theodora drew two clocks on the board — one on the ground, one on a fast-moving train. “Ask yourself: which clock is ‘really’ running slower? The answer is both — each measures the other’s clock as slower. There is no privileged frame, no absolute ‘really.’ That symmetry is the heart of special relativity.”
“But then — in the twin paradox, one twin actually comes back younger. So something breaks the symmetry?”

“Exactly right. The travelling twin accelerates — changes inertial frames. That breaks the symmetry. Special relativity handles constant-velocity frames; when you accelerate, you need general relativity. The traveller ages less not because of the journey’s speed alone, but because of the asymmetry introduced by the turnaround.”
“And gravitational time dilation — so GPS really needs Einstein, not Newton?”

“Every day. The satellites run fast due to weaker gravity, slow due to their velocity — net correction 38 microseconds per day. Without it, your location drifts by ten kilometres. Every time you navigate somewhere successfully, you are living inside a proof that GR is correct.”

“And the deepest lesson: Einstein did not build this from experiment alone. He started from a conceptual inconsistency — light’s speed is constant in Maxwell’s equations, but Galilean relativity would let you catch up with it. He chose to trust Maxwell and rethink everything else. That is how revolutions work.”

subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a 16-year-old why time passes more slowly for someone moving very fast relative to you. Use the light clock thought experiment to show where the mathematics comes from — and then give one real-world example that proves this is not just theory.
learningObjectives: State Einstein's two postulates of special relativity and explain why the second postulate conflicts with Galilean velocity addition
Apply the time dilation and length contraction formulae quantitatively, including calculation of the Lorentz factor γ
Explain how general relativity reconceives gravity as spacetime curvature and identify four observational confirmations of GR
Evaluate the limits of relativity theory and the conceptual challenges in reconciling GR with quantum mechanics
commonMistakes: Treating time dilation and length contraction as illusions or perceptual effects — they are real, frame-dependent measurements, not errors
Thinking E=mc² implies mass is converted to energy: mass and energy are equivalent forms of the same quantity, not different things that convert into each other
Applying time dilation without specifying which frame measures proper time — Δt₀ is always the frame where the clock is at rest
Conflating special relativity (inertial frames, constant velocity) with general relativity (acceleration, gravity) — SR cannot handle gravity correctly
assessmentCriteria: Can derive time dilation qualitatively from the light-clock thought experiment and apply the formula Δt=γΔt₀ to numerical problems
Can articulate the equivalence principle and explain how it motivates the geometric interpretation of gravity in GR
Can critically evaluate at least three experimental tests of GR, distinguishing what each observation tests and at what precision
Can discuss the conceptual limits of both SR and GR, including the incompatibility with quantum mechanics and the nature of singularities
subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
A spaceship travels from Earth to a star 12 light-years away at v = 0.8c, then returns at the same speed.

  1. Calculate the Lorentz factor γ for this speed. Show your working.
  2. How long does the return trip take according to observers on Earth (the “coordinate time”)?
  3. How much time elapses for the crew on the spaceship (the proper time Δt₀)? Use Δt₀ = Δt/γ.
  4. By how much do the travellers age less than Earth observers?
  5. From the crew’s perspective, the distance to the star is Lorentz-contracted. Calculate the contracted distance L they measure for the outward journey. Does their measured travel time × v equal this contracted distance? Verify.
  6. If the spaceship emits a radio signal at 100 MHz in its rest frame, what frequency would Earth observers detect as it moves away from them? (Use the relativistic Doppler formula: f_obs = f_source × √((1−β)/(1+β)), where β = v/c.)
subChunks.guidedPracticeModelAnswer:
1. Lorentz factor at v = 0.8c:
γ = 1/√(1 − 0.8²) = 1/√(1 − 0.64) = 1/√0.36 = 1/0.6 = 5/3 ≈ 1.667

2. Earth-frame travel time (coordinate time):
Distance (one way) = 12 light-years. At v = 0.8c, time one way = 12/0.8 = 15 years. Round trip = 30 years as measured on Earth.

3. Proper time for crew:
Δt₀ = Δt/γ = 30/1.667 = 18 years elapsed for the crew.

4. Age difference:
Earth observers age 30 years; crew ages 18 years. Difference = 12 years. The crew return 12 years younger than Earth-bound twins.

5. Contracted distance and verification:
L = L₀/γ = 12/1.667 = 7.2 light-years
Crew travel time (outward) = 18/2 = 9 years (half the 18-year round trip).
Crew’s speed × crew’s time = 0.8c × 9 years = 7.2 light-years ✓ — consistent.

6. Relativistic Doppler:
β = 0.8. f_obs = 100 × √((1−0.8)/(1+0.8)) = 100 × √(0.2/1.8) = 100 × √0.111 = 100 × 0.333 = 33.3 MHz.
The signal is significantly redshifted because the source is receding. (Note: on the return leg, the signal would be blueshifted to 300 MHz.)
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml:
Evaluate the following claim: “General relativity will eventually be shown to be wrong, just as Newton’s gravity was shown to be wrong by GR — so we should not take GR’s predictions too seriously.”

In your response: (a) Assess whether “Newton was wrong” is an accurate characterisation — what is the relationship between Newtonian gravity and GR? (b) Summarise the current experimental status of GR — what has it successfully predicted, and at what precision? (c) Identify the regime where GR is expected to break down and explain why. (d) Discuss whether expecting a theory to be superseded implies its current predictions should not be taken seriously. Draw on the history and philosophy of science in your answer.
subChunks.modelAnswer:
(a) Newton was ‘wrong’ — in what sense?
It is misleading to say Newton was simply wrong. Newtonian gravity is an extraordinarily accurate approximation in the regime of weak gravitational fields and low velocities. GR reduces to Newtonian gravity in that limit — the classical equations emerge as a special case. Newton’s theory is better described as incomplete: it fails where fields are strong (near black holes, neutron stars, the early universe) or where precision is extreme (GPS, gravitational waves). It does not fail for apple-dropping or satellite-launching at conventional speeds. Calling Newton “wrong” misrepresents how scientific progress works: theories are not usually overturned wholesale but subsumed as limiting cases.

(b) Experimental status of GR:
GR has been tested with extraordinary precision: (i) perihelion precession of Mercury — predicted to arcsecond precision; (ii) Eddington’s 1919 light deflection, now confirmed by VLBI to <0.04% of GR’s prediction; (iii) Pound-Rebka gravitational redshift, confirmed to 1%; (iv) Shapiro delay (light slowed near massive objects), confirmed to 0.002% by Cassini in 2003; (v) frame-dragging (Lense-Thirring effect), confirmed by Gravity Probe B; (vi) gravitational waves — LIGO/Virgo detections match GR waveform templates; (vii) binary pulsar timing decay (Hulse-Taylor), matches GR energy loss to 0.2%. No confirmed experimental deviation from GR exists in any weak-field or strong-field test conducted to date.

(c) Where GR breaks down:
GR predicts its own limits at singularities: the Big Bang (infinite density at t=0) and the centres of black holes (the Penrose-Hawking singularity theorems prove geodesic incompleteness under very general assumptions). At these points, curvature diverges and the equations lose predictive power. Additionally, GR is a classical theory and cannot describe the quantum behaviour of spacetime at the Planck scale (~10⁻³⁵ m, ~10⁻⁴³ s). A theory of quantum gravity is needed. Attempts (string theory, loop quantum gravity) exist but produce no unique testable predictions that have been confirmed. GR also does not explain dark matter or dark energy, which must be added by hand — though these are not failures of GR per se.

(d) Should we distrust GR because it will be superseded?
No — this is a philosophically confused position. The history of science shows that even superseded theories can be extremely reliable within their domain of applicability. We still use Newtonian mechanics for most engineering. If GR is eventually superseded, its successor will almost certainly reproduce GR’s predictions in the regimes where it has been tested. The empirical success of GR — across twelve orders of magnitude in length scale, confirmed by multiple independent methods — justifies very high confidence in its predictions within tested regimes. Expecting future refinement is not a reason for present scepticism; it is simply good scientific epistemology. The appropriate stance is to trust GR strongly in tested regimes, remain genuinely uncertain at untested scales, and actively seek the theory that resolves those limits.

rabbitHoleTerms.description: The four-dimensional mathematical framework (three spatial dimensions + time) in which the events of special relativity are represented — where the spacetime interval ds² = −c²dt² + dx² + dy² + dz² is invariant across all inertial frames.
The generalization of a straight line to curved spacetime — the path of shortest (or extremal) spacetime interval. Freely falling objects, including light, follow geodesics in GR.

The exact solution to Einstein's field equations for the spacetime geometry outside a spherically symmetric, non-rotating mass — from which the Schwarzschild radius r_s = 2GM/c² (the event horizon of a black hole) is derived.
The prediction of GR that a rotating mass drags spacetime around with it, like a ball spinning in honey — confirmed by Gravity Probe B (2011) and by LIGO observations of spinning black hole mergers.

The ten (coupled, nonlinear, partial differential) equations G_μν = (8πG/c⁴)T_μν that relate spacetime curvature (left side) to the distribution of matter and energy (right side) — the core mathematical statement of general relativity.

Stephen Hawking's prediction (1974) that black holes slowly evaporate by emitting thermal radiation due to quantum effects near the event horizon — not yet observed but central to the information paradox and quantum gravity debate.

questions.questionHtml: A particle travels at v = 0.6c relative to a laboratory. If the particle’s proper lifetime is 2.0 μs, what lifetime does a laboratory observer measure?

The Hulse-Taylor binary pulsar provided an indirect confirmation of gravitational wave emission by general relativity. Which of the following correctly describes what was measured and why it confirmed GR?
options: The orbital period of the pulsar pair was observed to decrease over decades at a rate matching GR’s prediction for energy loss via gravitational wave emission
Gravitational waves were directly detected as spacetime distortions stretching and squeezing a 4 km arm interferometer
The radio pulses from the pulsar were Doppler-shifted in a pattern that showed spacetime curvature around the neutron star
Light from the companion star was deflected by the pulsar’s gravitational field, matching GR’s lensing prediction
questions.correctAnswer: The orbital period of the pulsar pair was observed to decrease over decades at a rate matching GR’s prediction for energy loss via gravitational wave emission
questions.explanationHtml: Correct. As the system loses energy to gravitational waves, the orbit shrinks and the period decreases. The measured rate of period decrease matched GR’s quadrupole formula prediction to 0.2% — earning Hulse and Taylor the 1993 Nobel Prize.

questions.questionHtml: A student argues: “Since GPS works using special relativistic corrections alone, general relativistic gravitational time dilation must be negligible in practice.” Critically evaluate this claim.
options: The claim is false: the gravitational (GR) correction of +45 μs/day is larger than the velocity (SR) correction of −7 μs/day, making GR the dominant and essential correction for GPS accuracy
The claim is true: satellite velocities produce the main relativistic effect, while gravitational differences at GPS orbital altitude are too small to matter
The claim is partly correct: SR corrections are applied in real-time, while GR corrections are too complex to compute and are instead approximated by fixed offsets built into satellite hardware

The claim is false, but only for satellites in low Earth orbit — at GPS orbital altitude, SR effects dominate because the satellite moves faster relative to Earth’s surface than it would in higher orbits
questions.correctAnswer: The claim is false: the gravitational (GR) correction of +45 μs/day is larger than the velocity (SR) correction of −7 μs/day, making GR the dominant and essential correction for GPS accuracy
questions.explanationHtml: Correct. GPS satellites orbit at ~20,200 km altitude where gravity is weaker — GR predicts their clocks run fast by ~45 μs/day. SR slows them by ~7 μs/day due to velocity (~3.9 km/s). Net effect is +38 μs/day, mostly from GR. Without GR, GPS positions would accumulate ~10 km/day error. GR is indispensable.
